Chapter Two: The Onset of Persecution—Loss, Separation, and the Struggle to Endure.
Have you ever noticed how life can change in an instant? For this family, the shift was sudden and absolute. One day, the city felt familiar and safe. The next? It was like walking through a maze where every turn brought new dangers.
Suddenly, Jews were banned from parks, schools, even the benches in public squares. They had to wear marks that called them out, making them easy targets for harassment.
Imagine the apartment that once overflowed with laughter and warmth—now, it was quiet. Eerily quiet. Friends began to vanish, some sneaking away to other countries, others taken in the dead of night.
The girl’s father, who’d already lost his job and sense of purpose, grew sick. Money for medicine and food ran out fast. Her mother, ever resourceful, started selling the things she cherished just to keep them going. Every day brought some new rule, some fresh humiliation.
For the girl, now a young woman, dreams of becoming a lawyer slipped away. School was out of the question. Survival was all that mattered.
Then one morning, everything changed again. A letter arrived—cold and official. She was ordered to report for forced labor. There was no room for hope, no way to say no. So, she packed a small bag, hugged her mother tight, and boarded a train packed with others facing the same fate.
The camp was nothing like home. Days blended together—scrubbing floors, sorting vegetables, always under the watchful eyes of guards. Hunger was constant. But the fear? That was worse. Every single day, she wondered: would she ever see her family again?
But even in that harsh place, people found ways to connect. Strangers became friends, sharing tiny scraps of bread and whispered memories of home. Some clung to hope. Others, to anger. She quickly learned to keep her head down, to never stand out. Punishments came fast, and for no real reason.
Letters from home were her lifeline. Her mother wrote about the daily struggle—neighbors who wouldn’t look her in the eye, the endless hunt for food. The young woman wrote back, always careful with her words. She didn’t want to add to her mother’s worries, even though her own heart ached for comfort.
Then, without warning, the letters stopped. Days turned into weeks of silence. She replayed their last conversation over and over, desperate for any sign of hope. Not knowing was almost worse than knowing something bad.
One day, her name was called. Suddenly, she was being sent home—but not for freedom. She was told to prepare for deportation to the east. And everyone knew what that meant.
Returning to Vienna, she found her mother even thinner, even more anxious. They held each other, realizing that their time together might be short.
It’s in moments of desperation that people find hidden strength. The young woman and her mother searched for any possible escape. They reached out to friends, begged for help, and considered every risky option. Most doors slammed shut. But a few stayed open, just a crack.
A non-Jewish friend offered to hide her. But the risk was terrifying—if they were caught, both would pay with their lives.
Here’s something to think about: sometimes, surviving means letting go of everything you once believed made you who you are. The price is heartbreaking, but the alternative? It’s unthinkable.
